newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia adopts free-market labour system.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia adopts free-market labour system.

text.p: Australia, now under a conservative government after 13 years of Labor rule, on Tuesday adopted a new industrial relations system that emphasises free-market bargaining and a smaller role for unions.
Labor tried to block the new legislation in the upper house of parliament, the Senate, but the Liberal-National government combined with a minor party to push its bill through.

"If you want to achieve change as a nation, if you want to achieve change in industrial relations you have got to help build the new environment," government senator Ian Campbell told opposing politicians.
"You would prefer to keep Australia in the old environment, not to change it, not to move us forward at all," he said.

The old industrial environment was heavily regulated, although it was former prime minister Paul Keating's Labor government that took the first steps towards a more flexible system designed to lift Australia's economic growth rate.
In the early 1990s Keating encouraged unions and companies to build deals tailored to individual workplaces, trading off old-fashioned and inefficient work practices for more pay.
The new government, elected in March, takes that several steps further, for example by excluding unions from workplaces where the employees do not want them.
Keating downgraded labour courts from determining wage rates to merely approving employee-employer deals. Under the new system, the courts can have no say at all.

Prime Minister John Howard's government, elected in a landslide, came to office arguing that much more needed to be done to get the Australian economy moving, especially if it was to compete with its Asian neighbours.

Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith promised last month that the new labour system would result in more jobs and faster economic growth. But trade unionists have warned that the system would only cause more strikes.

On Tuesday afternoon, the bill's imminent passage prompted pre-emptive action from Australian waterfront workers, who walked off the job in all major ports to protest against the secondary boycott provisions contained in the new legislation.
Secondary boycott provisions prevent workers unconnected to a dispute from striking in support.
"This is draconian legislation," Maritime Union of Australia joint national secretary John Coombs said in a statement.
The controversial bill had a rough passage through the parliament, particularly in the non-government dominated Senate where it was subjected to almost 50 hours of debate.
It was eventually passed with 176 changes insisted on by the Australian Democrats minor party in return for its support.
The changes are now expected to take effect by February.
